analysis.one_liner: Bars health insurers from using "hold harmless" contract clauses to escape malpractice liability.
analysis.headline: A bill to bar insurers from using "hold harmless" clauses to escape malpractice liability was introduced in the House with no cosponsors and never got a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: Many health plans write contracts that say the insurer cannot be blamed — or sued for malpractice — when care the plan provides or withholds goes wrong; the liability is pushed onto doctors instead. This bill would ban those "hold harmless" provisions, letting patients sue the health plan itself over care decisions. It was sent to a House subcommittee and never went anywhere.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients injured by medical care provided or withheld under a managed care plan. Today, plans often use contract clauses to shift blame for denied or limited care onto doctors, leaving the patient unable to hold the plan accountable. The bill would let civil suits reach the health plan itself [S2][S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Patients hurt by managed care decisions

how_it_helps.text: The bill would prohibit health plans and insurer-provider contracts from containing clauses holding the plan harmless from liability in any civil action arising out of medical care provided or withheld under the plan [S2][S3].
Because HMOs and insurers are explicitly covered by the definition of insurer, patients could sue over care denied or managed by the plan rather than only suing the treating physician [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Health insurers and HMOs, which would face civil liability for care they provide or withhold, and could pass some of the resulting litigation and premium costs to consumers [S2].

drawbacks.text: Banning hold-harmless clauses could expose insurers and plans to more malpractice litigation, which insurers would likely pass on to consumers as higher premiums.

The bill was a one-page prohibition; it did not itself establish a cause of action against health plans, so even with hold-harmless clauses banned, patients could still face uncertainty about how to bring a claim.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit — giving injured patients a real path to sue their insurer — was real and focused. The costs would be additional litigation and potentially higher premiums, and the bill did nothing to address how a suit would be framed. As a one-page bill introduced without any cosponsors late in a session, its design was minimal and it never received committee or floor consideration, so its practical merits were never tested.

outcome.mechanism: The House referred it to the Commerce Committee, which sent it to a health subcommittee where it sat until the Congress ended, with no hearing, markup, or vote.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on June 20, 1996 and referred the same day to the House Committee on Commerce.
On June 28, 1996 it was referred to the Subcommittee on Health and Environment, where it stayed.
No further action was taken before the 104th Congress ended on January 3, 1997.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health insurers and HMOs, which kept the hold-harmless protection the bill would have removed.

against.name: House Commerce Committee / Subcommittee on Health and Environment
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referring it to the Subcommittee on Health and Environment; no hearing or markup is recorded.

against.name: Health insurance and managed care industry
against.what_they_did: Opposed expanding managed care liability during this era, arguing it would raise premiums; no action on this specific bill appears in the record.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a single Democratic sponsor, no cosponsors, and no recorded votes, so no partisan pattern can be read from the record.

industries.note: The bill would bar the hold-harmless clauses that insurers and HMOs used to shield themselves from malpractice liability for care they provided or withheld, exposing them to civil suits. Killing the bill preserved that protection.
Providers currently bear liability that contracts shift toward them; the bill would let some of that exposure be shared with plans. The effect on individual doctors was modest either way.
